title: Λύκος καὶ κύων
part: The Wolf and the Dog (Chambry 226 · Perry 346)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 226 (= Perry 346). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκος ἐν κλοιῷ δεδεμένον ὁρῶν μέγιστον κύνα ἤρετο· « Δήσας τίς σ’ ἐξέθρεψε τοῦτον ; »
sentences.tr: Lykos en kloiōi dedemenon horōn megiston kyna ēreto· « Dēsas tis s’ exethrepse touton ; »
sentences.l: A wolf, seeing a very large dog bound in a collar, asked: « Who, having tied you up, reared you to be this? »
sentences.i: A wolf, seeing a huge dog fastened in a collar, asked: « Who tied you up and reared you into what you are? »
sentences.n: δεδεμένον is a perfect passive participle — not the act of tying but the state of being tied. μέγιστος here is size, not eminence: an enormous dog. τοῦτον is a predicate accusative agreeing with σ(ε): reared you into this, i.e. to this size.

The answer is a single word, and the speech opens its guillemets here without closing them — Chambry runs the exchange on and marks the change of speaker with the dash at the head of the next sentence. Sentences that open « with no » (or close » with no «) are a regular feature of his page, not an error.

sentences.t: — Ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μὴ πάθοι λύκος ἐμοὶ φίλος· λιμὸς γὰρ ἡ κλοιοῦ βαρύτης. »
sentences.tr: — Alla touto mē pathoi lykos emoi philos· limos gar hē kloiou barytēs. »
sentences.l: — But may no wolf dear to me suffer this; for the weight of the collar is famine. »
sentences.n: The dash is Chambry's mark for the change of speaker; the wolf is talking again. πάθοι is an optative of wish, negatived by μή — the regular way of wishing a thing away. λιμός stands first as the predicate, for the point of the retort: the dog is fat, but a collar is a famine all the same.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ τὸ ἐν ταῖς συμφοραῖς οὐδὲ γαστρίζεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi to en tais symphorais oude gastrizesthai.
sentences.l: The story shows that one must not even gorge oneself in misfortunes.
sentences.n: The Greek is an articular infinitive, τὸ … γαστρίζεσθαι, standing as the object of δηλοῖ — word for word, 'the not-even-stuffing-oneself amid misfortunes.' γαστρίζομαι is to fill the belly full. The line can be heard either as advice (one ought not) or as a plain observation (in calamity there is no enjoying even a full belly); the wolf's own refusal in the fable pulls it toward the first.
